newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Rate cut still on despite strong Australian data.
newsitem.headline: Rate cut still on despite strong Australian data.

text.p: Australia's central bank was still likely to cut interest rates by early November despite signs from two key indicators that the economy remained strong, economists said on Tuesday.

Official statistics released on Tuesday showed that retail trade rose 1.1 percent in August, while building approvals were up 1.6 percent in the same month. Both results were stronger than the market expected.
Economists had forecast a fall of about 1.2 percent in retail trade, while building approvals were expected to rise only 1.0 percent.
"The case for a rate cut has not been undermined by today's data," Citibank senior economist Stephen Koukoulas said.
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) held its monthly board meeting on Tuesday, but was not expected to have decided on another reduction in rates, economists said.
Even so, financial market traders will nervously watch their trading screens at 9.30 a.m. (2330 GMT) on Wednesday when monetary policy statements are usually released.
Tempering the strength in August retail trade, seen by economists as the more important figure, was a downward revision in the July figure to a 1.0 percent rise from the original rise of 2.4 percent.
It was the first time in two years that retail sales had risen 1.0 percent or more in successive months.
"It is, however, a little premature to view this as the dawn of a new upswing in consumer spending," Bankers Trust Australia chief economist Chris Caton said.
The building approvals data showed a welcome rise. But the housing sector was still some time away from a full recovery, although some positive signs were emerging, he said.
Colonial State Bank senior economist Craig James said the data suggested "a modest housing recovery is under way."
"Recovery in the housing sector is likely to remain modest while the job market is subdued and consumers are less confident," James said.
Economists said both sets of data confirmed that while the economy was not falling over, it was patchy and may need an interest rate cut to boost activity.

They said the most likely time for another cut was at the end of October or after the next RBA monthly board meeting on November 5, when the central bank will have received September employment and third quarter inflation and wages data.
"I think the inflation numbers remain pretty favourable for another rate cut," ANZ Treasury economist Karen Pringle said.
"If we see further softness in employment, that's probably going to determine whether or not we get the rate cut in November that we are in fact predicting," she said.
The RBA cut rates by 50 basis points to 7.00 percent on July 31, citing the low inflation outlook and concern about high unemployment.
